d: Consolidated overview of cross-platform recommendations to help you design a Roblox game that's accessible and enjoyable on all platforms.
h:
import BetaAlert from '../includes/beta-features/beta-alert.md'

Roblox is inherently cross‑platform, as players can discover and join games on their phone or tablet, then later continue where they left off on their PC or console. To support an expanding suite of platforms, you should build user interfaces that seamlessly adapt to the input type (touch, gamepad, mouse/keyboard), screen size, and device orientation. This guide, the adaptive design guide, and the linked resources can help you design a true cross‑platform game that's compatible, accessible, and enjoyable on all platforms.

To explore a pre-made game that showcases the following cross‑platform design concepts, check out the Interactivity Showcase.

Input

A carefully designed game should support all primary input types, including mouse and keyboard, touch, and gamepads.

Cross-platform actions

Support all primary input types (mouse/keyboard, touch, and gamepads) using the Input Action System.

To simplify cross‑platform inputs, Roblox provides the Input Action System to define actions such as "jump," "sprint," or "shoot" and set up bindings for multiple hardware inputs to drive those actions. You do not need to think about all the technical aspects of hardware inputs and when to listen for specific input triggers; you simply define which inputs perform which actions.

Input type detection

Ensure that UI elements respond and adapt to the player's primary input type as detailed in input type detection. Also consider assistive hints to help players understand specific input changes.

In cross-platform development, it's important that you determine and respond to the primary input type a player is using, normally to ensure that UI elements like on‑screen buttons and menus work elegantly and support interaction across devices.

For example, a touch‑enabled device assumes touch is the default input and that touch buttons may appear for actions, but a player may choose to connect a bluetooth gamepad. In this case, touch remains a valid input, but you can assume the player wants to switch to the connected gamepad as the primary input type and possibly use touch as a backup input for on‑screen UI.

If you're using the Input Action System, the PreferredBinding property complements primary input detection: just as PreferredInput reports the player's current primary input type, PreferredBinding reports the specific InputBinding that matches the player's current device. Both update automatically as the player switches devices, so you can drive device‑aware UI without writing device‑switch logic yourself.

Assistive hints

Based on the primary input type, it's recommended that you include assistive UI hints whenever possible. For example, when selecting tools to equip, display input‑specific hints such as 1–5 when the player is using a keyboard, or gamepad trigger hints when the player is using a gamepad.

For no-code assistive hints that automatically update when the player switches devices, use InputActionLabel and point it at any InputAction to display the correct input per platform. See displaying bindings for full details.

For more granular control, or if you need to customize hint display beyond what InputActionLabel offers, you can use the UserInputService methods below to manually gather platform‑specific images and strings:

The GetImageForKeyCode() and GetStringForKeyCode() methods are helpful in gathering a platform‑specific image or string to use in a UI hint, such as the following examples:

Key Code Xbox Image PlayStation Image String
KeyCode.ButtonA `ButtonA`
KeyCode.ButtonX `ButtonX`
KeyCode.One n/a n/a `1`
KeyCode.Five n/a n/a `5`

User interface

A well-designed user interface is essential for players on all platforms to interact with your game.

Position and size

Ensure that all UI elements are visible on all screen sizes and orientations.

Ensure that all buttons/controls are interactable and that they are not blocked or obscured by device cutouts or Roblox UI elements.

All UI elements should be positioned and sized appropriately to ensure visibility and interactivity across multiple screen sizes. Positioning UI elements by Scale is a common approach since it's based on a percentage of the screen's X and Y bounds, not a pixel value (pixels can vary arbitrarily by both number and density across devices). You can also utilize the element's AnchorPoint to set its positional origin. For example, the UI container holding the gem/coin counters in the following image is positioned at an X scale of 1 (right) and Y scale of 0 (top) with an upper‑right anchor point.

Scale is also recommended for sizing UI elements, such as making a UI container span 75% width on every screen. However, 75% would render to a huge size on 4K TVs for console players, so it's recommended that you explore screen size adaptation as a way to adapt UI layouts across different viewports.

Screen size adaptation

Adapt UI to various display sizes by checking and listening for changes to the viewport display size.

With a multitude of possible screen sizes accessible to the Roblox platform, attempting to predict screen size by pixels often leads to misinterpretation. To assist in determining a player's screen size to adapt the size/position of UI elements, Roblox provides the read‑only ViewportDisplaySize property which represents the internally‑categorized rendering size of the viewport.

ViewportDisplaySize Summary
Small Most tablet/mobile/handheld devices
Medium Most laptops and monitors
Large Most TVs or larger

For more native customization, you can use the UI Style Editor to configure Style Queries for both ViewportDisplaySize and PreferredInput values. Using intrinsic selectors like @ViewportDisplaySizeSmall or @PreferredInputTouch allows your UI to automatically swap tokens for text sizes, container dimensions, and other measurements as the player's device environment or primary input method changes.

Layout containers

Use layouts to organize individual UI components and ensure that containers adjust responsively to the children elements within them.

For easier UI organization, you should use layout components to organize children. When using layout containers, make sure that the children are legible, accessible, and non‑cluttered. A common layout component is UIListLayout, which positions sibling GuiObjects into rows or columns and adjusts accordingly whenever you add or remove a sibling object.

You should also consider the distribution and relative positioning of elements within layout containers for the best user experience. Integrating flex into a list layout is a powerful way to equally fill/distribute or align/stretch items across their line, or flex specific items across a variable space.

Accessibility

Ensure that all text is legible on all screens. Also make sure all UI has sufficient contrast and that nothing relies solely on color to distinguish an action or outcome.

Even with UI elements properly sized across all device screen sizes, the overall game should meet accessibility standards for players with impaired vision or color blindness. Text size can factor heavily into the legibility of text‑based UI, so you should include a text size constraint to ensure text doesn't become illegible (too small) or visually too large on larger screens like 4K TVs.

For more tips on accessibility, see accessibility guidelines.

Final tips & tricks

As you work toward a full cross‑platform game, consider the following tips and tricks:

  • Device emulation is essential to designing an optimal game on Roblox. Utilize the built‑in Device Emulator and Controller Emulator to emulate various devices and gamepads directly in Studio.
  • Roblox's UI styling pipeline, similar to CSS, lets you declare and globally apply overrides to UI instance properties. Along with the integrated Style Editor, you can set up a complete and easy‑to‑modify user interface.
  • Once your game is effectively cross-platform, explore native features like haptic feedback on mobile and gamepads, touch gestures such as TouchSwipe and TouchPinch, or accelerometer and gyroscope functionality on AccelerometerEnabled and GyroscopeEnabled devices.

kid.simple: Roblox players join from phones, tablets, computers, consoles, and more, sometimes switching devices in the middle of a week. This page gives tips so your game works well on all of them: support every kind of control, show the right button hints, and make your UI fit every screen size. A game that only works well on a PC loses everyone playing on a phone or Xbox, which is a huge part of Roblox.
kid.analogy: It is like a restaurant that serves people who are right-handed, left-handed, eating with chopsticks, or using a fork. A good restaurant gives everyone the right tool and a table that fits, instead of making them all use the same thing.
keyPoints: Support all main inputs: mouse and keyboard, touch, and gamepads (controllers).
The Input Action System lets you name actions like jump or sprint, then connect many inputs to each one, so you do not write separate code for each device.
`UserInputService.PreferredInput` tells you which input the player mainly uses right now, like Touch or Gamepad, and it updates when they switch.
Show hints that match the device, like 1 to 5 on a keyboard or trigger icons on a gamepad. `InputActionLabel` can do this with no code.
Place and size UI using Scale (a percentage of the screen) instead of pixels, and use AnchorPoint to set which corner a UI element is pinned by.
`GuiService.ViewportDisplaySize` sorts the screen into Small (most phones and tablets), Medium (most laptops and monitors), or Large (most TVs).
Use layouts like `UIListLayout` to line up buttons in rows or columns that adjust automatically when you add or remove items.
Keep text readable on all screens, use enough color contrast, and never use only color to show meaning. Test with Studio's Device Emulator and Controller Emulator.

terms.cross-platform: Working on many kinds of devices, like phone, PC, console, and VR.
terms.input: How a player controls the game: keys, mouse clicks, screen taps, or controller buttons.
terms.gamepad: A game controller, like an Xbox or PlayStation controller.
terms.binding: A link between a real button (like Space or ButtonA) and an action (like jump).
terms.primary input type: The control the player is mainly using right now. A tablet with a controller plugged in may switch from Touch to Gamepad.
terms.assistive hint: A small on-screen picture or text that shows which button to press, like a little A icon.
terms.Scale: A size or position measured as a fraction of the screen. An X scale of 0.5 means halfway across, no matter if the screen is 800 or 3000 pixels wide.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on a screen. Different devices have very different numbers of pixels, so pixel sizes look different on each.
terms.AnchorPoint: The point on a UI element that its position refers to. With AnchorPoint (1, 0), the element's top-right corner sits at its position, so position X scale 1, Y scale 0 puts it snug in the top-right corner of the screen.
terms.viewport: The area of the screen where the game is shown.
terms.layout: An object, like `UIListLayout`, that automatically arranges the UI items next to it in rows or columns.
terms.contrast: How different two colors look. White text on black has high contrast and is easy to read; light gray on white is hard.
terms.emulator: A Studio tool that pretends to be another device, like a phone or controller, so you can test without owning it.
terms.haptic feedback: Vibration from a phone or controller to make actions feel real.

example.title: Show the right jump hint for the player's device
example.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UserInputService = game:GetService("UserInputService")

local player = Players.LocalPlayer

-- Make a simple hint label at the bottom of the screen
local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.ResetOnSpawn = false
screenGui.Parent = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local hint = Instance.new("TextLabel")
hint.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 1)          -- pin by bottom-middle
hint.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.95)      -- 50% across, 95% down
hint.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.3, 0.06)          -- 30% wide, 6% tall
hint.TextScaled = true
hint.Parent = screenGui

-- Change the text to match the main input type
local function updateHint()
	local input = UserInputService.PreferredInput
	if input == Enum.PreferredInput.Gamepad then
		hint.Text = "Press A to jump"
	elseif input == Enum.PreferredInput.Touch then
		hint.Text = "Tap the jump button"
	else
		hint.Text = "Press Space to jump"
	end
end

updateHint()
-- Update again if the player switches devices
UserInputService:GetPropertyChangedSignal("PreferredInput"):Connect(updateHint)
explain: We create a ScreenGui and a TextLabel inside the player's PlayerGui so the hint shows on their screen.
The label uses Scale, so it is 30% of the screen wide on any device, and AnchorPoint (0.5, 1) keeps it centered at the bottom.
`updateHint` reads `PreferredInput` and picks the right words for gamepad, touch, or keyboard.
We call it once at the start, then again whenever `PreferredInput` changes, like when a tablet player connects a controller.

watchOut: Sizing UI in pixels. A 400-pixel-wide button can be huge on a phone and tiny on a 4K TV. Use Scale and test with the Device Emulator.
Using Scale only, with no limits. 75% of a TV screen is enormous. Adapt by `ViewportDisplaySize` or add size constraints.
Putting buttons in corners where phone notches or Roblox's own buttons cover them. Check that every button can still be tapped.
Showing keyboard hints like Press E to a phone or console player. Match hints to the player's main input.
